claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is favored when precursor mobility is inhibited during formation.
Mobility inhibition forces nearly simultaneous, stochastic reduction and nucleation of all metal species.
Nearly simultaneous stochastic formation prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
The initial material is a dispersed mixture of noble metal salts or single-source precursors prior to reduction.
Rapid quenching or shortening the reaction window can restrict atomic diffusion during reduction and nucleation.
The proposed mechanism operates in low-to-moderate-temperature synthesis of noble metal HEA nanoparticles.
At low-to-moderate temperatures, reduction kinetics are slow enough to be influenced by atomic-mobility constraints.
The mechanism should not apply in extreme high-temperature regimes such as plasma-based synthesis because the thermal pulse dominates formation.
Limited mobility of metal atoms during nucleation and growth is the structural mediator.
Stochastic formation rather than sequential or mobile incorporation causes all constituent metals to nucleate nearly simultaneously.
Limiting mobility suppresses phase separation and favors formation of a single HEA phase.
With higher mobility, differences among metal reduction kinetics promote segregated phases or uncontrolled morphologies.
Mobility-inhibited nanoparticles will have a spatially uniform and homogeneous distribution of their noble metals.
The mobility-inhibited material will exhibit consistent lattice parameters and elemental maps.
The unchanged, higher-mobility baseline is more likely to produce phase-separated, compositionally segregated, or morphologically irregular nanoparticles.
The hypothesis applies specifically when reduction kinetics control alloy-phase formation.
The exact degree of mobility inhibition required for successful formation is unknown.
Ligands and support interactions may also affect HEA nanoparticle formation in practical implementations.
